hint: Marie is one person, so use the 'she has' form of avoir (to have), then the past form of lire (to read).
explanation: The past form of lire (to read) is lu. With Marie, use a (the 'she has' form of avoir) followed by lu, so it means she read.

wrong_answer_feedback.sommes vu: Voir (to see) uses avoir (to have) as its helper word, not être (to be).
wrong_answer_feedback.avons voir: After avoir, you need the past form vu, not the infinitive voir (to see).
wrong_answer_feedback.avons voyé: The past form of voir (to see) is vu, not a -é form like voyé.

hint: Work out which helper word goes with voir (to see), then use the past form of voir.
explanation: Voir (to see) takes avoir, and its past form is vu: nous avons vu means we saw or we have seen. Check the helper word first, then the past form.

hint: Use j'ai (I have) with the past form of finir (to finish).
explanation: Use j'ai (I have) plus the past form of finir (to finish), which is fini. Mes devoirs means my homework.

hint: Look at the verb that comes after j'ai. After avoir, it needs its past form, which for -er verbs ends in a specific letter.
explanation: After avoir (to have), the verb must be in its past form, not the plain infinitive. For -er verbs such as manger (to eat), that form ends in -é.

hint: Aller (to go) uses être (to be) as its helper word, and Sophie is a woman, so pick the matching form of être for 'she is'.
explanation: Aller (to go) uses être (to be) as its helper word, so the sentence means she went. The -ée ending on allée matches Sophie being a woman.

prompt: Mes parents ___ partis à huit heures.

wrong_answer_feedback.ont: Partir (to leave) uses être (to be) as its helper word, not avoir (to have).
wrong_answer_feedback.est: Mes parents means more than one person, so the helper word needs the plural form.

hint: Partir (to leave) is a verb of going away, so it takes être. Think about which form of être fits more than one person.
explanation: Partir (to leave) takes être, so use sont (they are) with the past form partis: mes parents sont partis. The -s on partis shows there is more than one person.

hint: Marie is a woman. Check whether the past form needs an extra ending for a woman.
explanation: Arriver (to arrive) takes être, and when the person is a woman the past form gets an extra -e. So Marie is arrivée.

hint: Rentrer (to go back home) takes être. Your grandmother is a woman, so the past form needs the ending for a woman.
explanation: Rentrer (to go back home) takes être, so the past form must match a woman, which adds an -e. Revenir (to come back) also works in this sentence.

prompt: Quand Paul était petit, il ___ (jouer) au foot.
hint: The sentence describes a habit from childhood, so use the form of jouer (to play) that means 'used to' for il (he).
explanation: The 'used to' past form describes what someone regularly did. For il (he) with jouer (to play), it is jouait, meaning he used to play.

prompt: Quand j'étais enfant, nous ___ à la mer tous les étés.

wrong_answer_feedback.irons: Irons is the future form (we will go), but the sentence is about a habit in the past.
wrong_answer_feedback.allons: Allons is the present form, meaning we go, but the sentence is about when you were a child.

hint: The sentence is about your childhood and a repeated habit. Use the 'used to' form of aller (to go) for nous (we).
explanation: The 'used to' past form describes things that happened regularly. Nous allions means we used to go, or we would go, every summer.
review_notes: Original prompt had no past cue so 'allons' was also correct; added childhood cue, replaced 'sommes allés' with 'irons' and updated feedback/hint.

hint: Autrefois means in the past, so the verb needs the 'used to' form for nous (we), not the present form.
explanation: Autrefois (in the past) tells you to use the 'used to' form. For nous (we) with habiter (to live), that is habitions, not habitons.

prompt: The weather was cold in the mountains.
acceptable_alternatives: Il faisait froid à la montagne.
Il faisait froid dans les montagnes.
hint: French describes the weather with faire (literally 'to do' or 'to make') and il (it). Use its past 'description' form, the same one as 'used to'.
explanation: The weather in the past is described with faire: il faisait means it was (weather). Il faisait froid means it was cold.
flags: ai-review: passe compose "Il a fait froid en montagne" is also a defensible translation of "was cold"; imperfect is the intended target but the prompt does not force it

prompt: Tu prends le bus ? Oui, je ___ prends.
hint: Replace the bus with a short word that means it and goes just before the verb prends.
explanation: Le stands in for a masculine thing such as the bus, and it goes right before the verb: je le prends means I take it.

prompt: Tu écris à ta sœur ? Oui, je ___ écris souvent.

wrong_answer_feedback.la: La stands for a thing or person being acted on directly, but writing to someone needs a word meaning to her.
wrong_answer_feedback.leur: Leur means to them, so it fits a group of people, not one sister.

hint: Your sister is one person, and you need a short word before the verb that means to her.
explanation: Écrire à (to write to) someone uses lui (to him or to her) before the verb: je lui écris means I write to her. Leur is used for to them.

hint: The short word for it goes before the verb, not after it.
explanation: Short words such as le go in front of the verb, so je le vois means I see it. The time word demain (tomorrow) goes at the end.
flags: supervisor: English prompt 'I see it tomorrow.' is unnatural; consider 'I'm seeing him tomorrow.' (le = him/it)

acceptable_alternatives: Je suis en train de leur écrire.
hint: Put the short word for to them before the verb écrire (to write), using je (I).
explanation: Leur means to them and goes before the verb: je leur écris means I write to them. Je suis en train de leur écrire is a longer way to say the same thing.

prompt: Which sentence means 'I have a headache'?

Tête goes with à la, as in la tête, so au is the wrong word here.
That means I have a sore throat, not a headache.

hint: Find the sentence that names the part of the body above your neck, where your brain is.
explanation: J'ai mal à la tête means my head hurts. Use à la with la words such as la tête (the head).

acceptable_alternatives: I have a pain in my back.
hint: Dos is the part of your body behind your chest, and mal means pain or an ache.
explanation: Mal au dos means pain in the back. Au is the form of à used with le words, and le dos is the back.

hint: Start with où (where), then use the form of être (to be) that fits one place.
explanation: Où est means where is. For a single place such as la pharmacie (the pharmacy), use est (is).

hint: Use j'ai mal for hurts. Pied is a le word, so pick the short form of à that goes with le.
explanation: Mal au pied means pain in the foot. Au joins à and le, and is used before le words such as le pied (the foot).
